newsitem.title: JAPAN: Temperature rises in global warming debate.
newsitem.headline: Temperature rises in global warming debate.

text.p: Bonn had the environmental spotlight on Friday as officials from around the world met to hash out a plan for reducing greenhouse gases ahead of this December's conference on climate change in the western Japan city of Kyoto.

But ministerial meetings in Tokyo between Australia and Japan, the conference host, cast an even stronger light on the great divide still separating developed countries from agreement on how to fight global warming.

In a joint news conference on Friday, officials from both Tokyo and Canberra stressed their view that the stance of the European Union, which champions a uniform 15 percent cut in the emissions from 1990 levels by 2010, was both extreme and inequitable.
"I hardly see how it is practical to reduce (greenhouse) gases by such a large margin," said Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
"And with such a lack of equity between requirements for EU and non-EU members, it may be difficult to find agreement," he added.

At the heart of the debate are what conference officials call quantified emission limitation and reduction objectives, or QELROs -- specific numerical targets for emission cuts, in common parlance and the raison d'etre of the Kyoto meeting.

Under the EU proposal, EU member states would be allowed to determine different targets for emission cuts on a country-by-country basis, with emissions from some European countries actually increasing.
Non-EU members, meanwhile, would all be held to a flat 15 percent reduction.
"It's obviously not fair to ask some countries to shoulder more of the burden than others," said Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer.
International views on the targets are wide-ranging.

Not surprisingly, a small but vocal group known as the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), has proposed an even greater cut than the EU, insisting that emitted greenhouse gases drop by 20 percent from 1990 levels by 2005.

Their concerns arise from forecasts that rising sea levels -- an estimated 50 cm by 2100 -- will subsume significant areas of low-lying land masses as pollutants in the air lead to global temperature gains of up to four degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and a subsequent melting in the polar ice caps.
Major oil producing countries, meanwhile, are concerned that cuts in emissions will limit consumption of oil and have proposed that they be compensated for any lost sales.
Australia, which exports some 65 million tonnes of coal to Japan annually, has applied steady pressure on Japan to oppose the EU target.

The Kyoto conference, officially titled the Third Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP3, represents the deadline for developed nations to sign a protocol on legally binding targets.

Following that, under the latest proposal carried by the Japanese delegation to Bonn this week, the COP3 agreement would go into force only after both of two conditions are met -- that 50 countries ratify it within their own governments and that the countries which have ratified were collectively responsible for emitting at least 75 percent of total hydrocarbon pollutants in 1990.
